name: Testicular Cancer
aliases: Germ cell tumor of the testis

clinicalPearls: Germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for about 95% of all testicular neoplasms; non-GCTs of the testis are much less common, and roughly 5% of GCTs arise in extragonadal sites such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pineal gland.
Testicular cancer is regarded as a model curable neoplasm: about 95% of newly diagnosed patients are cured, and treatment is dictated by pathology (seminoma vs nonseminoma) and stage.
It is the most common malignancy in adolescent and young adult males (age 15-39), most often diagnosed in Caucasians and much less common in African Americans; incidence in those over 50 is rising.

Strongest risk factors are a prior history of GCT, cryptorchidism, and germ cell neoplasia in situ; a prior GCT carries a 1-2% risk of a contralateral tumor (usually metachronous), and cryptorchidism raises risk roughly four- to sixfold.
Orchidopexy before puberty reduces but does not eliminate the cryptorchidism-associated risk, and the contralateral normally descended testis also remains at risk.

A solid mass on scrotal ultrasound (typically hypoechoic, sometimes multifocal) must be considered malignant until proven otherwise; transscrotal aspiration or biopsy must never be performed because it risks seeding the scrotum or inguinal nodes.

Tumor marker biology is key: seminomas never secrete AFP, so a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP is managed as a nonseminomatous GCT; hCG can be elevated in both seminoma and nonseminoma, and choriocarcinoma may produce markedly high hCG.

Serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) should be measured before and after orchiectomy; AFP is elevated in roughly 60-70% of nonseminomatous GCTs, while most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation.

Lymphatic spread follows a predictable pattern: left-sided tumors drain first to left paraaortic nodes below the left renal vessels, right-sided tumors to aortocaval nodes below the right renal vessels, then to retrocrural, mediastinal, and supraclavicular nodes; the lung is the most common hematogenous site.
Genetically, most GCTs show excess copies of isochromosome 12p (i[12p]); the strongest heritable-risk locus identified is KITLG (KIT ligand) on chromosome 12, and overall heritability is nearly 50%.
Teratoma is chemotherapy-resistant and must be managed surgically; the other nonseminomatous subtypes (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma) and seminomas are chemosensitive.

Sperm banking should be offered before chemotherapy: about 30% of newly diagnosed patients already have severe oligospermia or azoospermia, and treatment-related sterility is common (though ~80% recover spermatogenesis over years).
harrison.pathophysiology: GCTs originate from the primordial germ cell, and most malignant GCTs arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ; the precise molecular steps driving progression from in situ neoplasia to invasive tumor are not fully defined. Genetic analysis shows excess copy number of isochromosome 12p in most cases, and genome-wide studies implicate several loci, most strongly KITLG on chromosome 12. Tumors are classified as seminoma (must be 100% seminoma; any mixed tumor is treated as nonseminomatous) or nonseminoma. Seminomas may contain syncytiotrophoblastic cells that secrete hCG but never secrete AFP. Nonseminomatous subtypes include embryonal carcinoma (the most undifferentiated, able to differentiate into the others, and may secrete AFP and/or hCG), yolk sac tumor (often AFP-secreting), choriocarcinoma (aggressive, often very high hCG), and teratoma (mature, immature, or malignant somatic tissue derived from two or more germ layers).
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary persistence of AFP or hepatic disease (false AFP elevation)
infectionMimics: Epididymitis (a trial of antibacterials may be considered, but failure to respond should prompt scrotal ultrasound)
nonInfectiousMimics: Hereditary persistence of AFP (mildly elevated baseline AFP)
Hepatic disease causing false AFP elevation
False hCG elevation from hypogonadism, marijuana use, or assay interference
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound of both testicles (GCT typically hypoechoic, possibly multifocal)
Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH before and after orchiectomy
CT scan of abdomen and pelvis for staging
Chest x-ray, with chest CT if retroperitoneal disease or lung nodules are present
Pathologic review of the entire orchiectomy specimen by an experienced pathologist
Serum microRNA miR-371a-3p (a promising investigational biomarker undergoing validation)
redFlags: Painless testicular mass (pathognomonic of GCT) or testicular swelling, firmness, or discomfort
Back or flank pain suggesting retroperitoneal metastases
Cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis indicating lung metastases
Gynecomastia in the setting of elevated hCG
Suspected epididymitis/orchitis that fails to respond to antibiotics
Rapidly progressive disease with life-threatening symptoms (e.g., hemoptysis) warranting emergent treatment even without tissue diagnosis
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes are excellent overall, with about 95% of newly diagnosed patients cured. Nearly all stage I patients (seminoma and nonseminoma) achieve cure. In metastatic (stage III) disease classified by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification, most patients have good-risk disease with >90% cure; intermediate- and poor-risk groups have approximately 80% and 50% five-year survival, respectively. About 20-30% of patients with metastatic GCT treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy do not achieve durable control, with most relapses occurring within 2 years of completing treatment.
pitfalls: Performing transscrotal biopsy or aspiration of a testicular mass, which can seed the scrotum or inguinal nodes and should never be done.
Misclassifying a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP as a true seminoma, when it must be approached as a nonseminomatous GCT.
Over-relying on tumor markers for diagnosis, since most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation.
Diagnostic delay (not uncommon) leading to more advanced stage at presentation, including mislabeling a GCT as epididymitis/orchitis.

Assuming residual postchemotherapy masses are benign: imaging cannot distinguish necrosis/fibrosis from teratoma or viable tumor, and enlarging cystic retroperitoneal masses with normalized markers may represent growing teratoma syndrome.
Forgetting that LDH is a nonspecific marker whose main role is risk classification in metastatic disease, not diagnosis.
harrison.severityClassification: Three main AJCC TNM-based stages: Stage I limited to the testis; Stage II involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes (subgrouped IIA/IIB/IIC by node size: <=2 cm, >2-5 cm, >5 cm); Stage III with lymph node involvement beyond the retroperitoneum and/or distant metastases. Stage III is further stratified into good-, intermediate-, and poor-risk groups by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification using histology, primary site, presence of nonpulmonary visceral metastases, and postorchiectomy marker levels (e.g., for NSGCT good-risk: AFP <1000 ng/mL, hCG <5000 mIU/mL, LDH <1.5x ULN; poor-risk: AFP >10,000 ng/mL, hCG >50,000 mIU/mL, LDH >10x ULN, mediastinal primary, or nonpulmonary visceral metastases). Marker half-lives: AFP 5-7 days, hCG 24-36 hours.
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy for diagnosis and local control, never a trans-scrotal biopsy which risks tumour seeding
Offer sperm banking before orchidectomy or systemic therapy, as both disease and treatment threaten fertility

Direct subsequent treatment by histology and stage: active surveillance for many stage I tumours, cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy such as BEP for metastatic disease, and radiotherapy as an option for seminoma
Consider retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection for selected non-seminomatous tumours or residual post-chemotherapy masses
Track serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH before and serially after treatment to guide staging, response and relapse detection
Maintain long-term surveillance for relapse, a metachronous contralateral tumour, and late effects of platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Provide androgen replacement if hypogonadal after treatment and manage within a uro-oncology multidisciplinary team
